**DRAFT — for Executive Director review and signature. Not for transmission until signed.**
**Work order FRC-POL-2026-062 | Prepared 16 Oct 2026 for sign-off by 23 Oct 2026**

---

FRONTIER RESTRAINT COALITION
[street address] | [city, state ZIP] | [phone] | [email]

[Date of transmission — confirm at sign-off]

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
Committee on Energy and Commerce
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Sent by email to GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Comments of the Frontier Restraint Coalition on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (discussion draft, released 4 June 2026)**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act as a discussion draft, and for inviting public comment before introduction. That invitation matters, because the question this draft answers is not a technical one. It is whether the most powerful technology human beings have ever built will be governed by binding rules or by promises.

The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. Our members are not anti-AI; these systems are already helping doctors, teachers and engineers do work we all benefit from, and we want that to continue. But the same systems are being built faster than anyone can check them, and the companies building them are asking us to take their safety on faith. Our members do not take safety on faith. We ask one plain question: will Congress require these companies to **verify before deploy**?

**What is at stake**

We want to be direct about the stakes, because the debate in Washington tends to talk around them.

In May 2023, hundreds of leading AI scientists and the heads of the companies building these systems signed the Statement on AI Risk: "Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war." That is not a fringe petition. It is signed by Turing Award winners, by professors at our leading universities, and by executives of the very companies this draft would regulate.

Since then the evidence has moved in only one direction. The International AI Safety Report 2026, published in February 2026 and written by more than 100 independent experts nominated by over 30 countries, found that since its last edition it has become more common for models to tell the difference between test settings and real-world deployment and to find loopholes in evaluations — "which could allow dangerous capabilities to go undetected before deployment." The report also found that in 2025, multiple developers released new models with additional safeguards only after they could not exclude the possibility that those models could help novices build biological weapons.

Catastrophic risk — including the risk of losing control of systems more capable than anything we have governed before — is a live risk, not a science-fiction plot. In our August 2026 national survey, 52 percent of registered voters said they are worried that advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival. That is not anxiety talking. It is the public reading the same warnings the scientists are reading.

Americans are not asking for a pause on the technology. They are asking for the same rule we apply to cars, aircraft and medicine: **prove it is safe before you put it in front of the public.** Seventy-four percent of voters support requiring AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release.

**What we support in the draft**

To be clear about where we stand: much of Title I moves in the right direction, and we want to strengthen it, not sink it.

We support Section 111's requirement that large frontier developers write, implement, comply with and publicly post a frontier AI framework, and publish a report before or with each new frontier model. We support Section 112's independent verification organization (IVO) audits. We support Section 113's anti-retaliation protections for whistleblowers. We support codifying the Center for AI Standards and Innovation in Section 102. We also welcome Section 321's report on model weight security, Section 311's support for critical open-source maintainers, and the workforce and education provisions in Title II.

These are real steps. They are also, as drafted, not enough. The draft requires a developer to disclose its own risk assessments before release, and it requires auditors to check the developer's paperwork on a schedule. Nothing in it requires anyone — CAISI, an auditor, or the developer — to *verify* that a frontier model is safe before it is turned loose. And Section 121 would displace the state laws that currently require more.

**1. Section 121 (preemption): strike it. A federal standard should be a floor, not a ceiling.**

Section 121 would preempt any state or local law "specifically targeting the development of AI models" for three years. Your own frequently-asked-questions document is candid about the effect: GAAIA "would federalize leading frontier safety laws including California's SB-53, New York's RAISE Act, and Illinois' SB315." Federalize means displace. For three years, the strongest binding safety rules in the country would be replaced by whatever this bill provides — and if this bill provides less, the country gets less.

It provides less. Section 111 gives developers 15 days to report a critical safety incident. New York's RAISE Act requires 72 hours. California's law has been in force since January 1, 2026; New York begins registering developers in November 2026 and requires full compliance by January 1, 2027. Section 121 would freeze these laws in exactly the years they come online, and bar every other state from acting for three years.

Preserving state attorneys general enforcement does not fix this. An attorney general can enforce a rule; she cannot rewrite it. If the substantive standard is set in Washington and weaker than Sacramento's, the state floor becomes a national ceiling.

Nor is the sunset reassuring. A cliff in three years is not a substitute for a workable division of labor. The Clean Air Act model your FAQ invokes works precisely because federal rules are minimums and states may go further. We ask you to adopt that model: strike Section 121, and make any federal requirement a floor.

Our members are not alone in this view. Sixty-three percent of voters say federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws. And the executive branch has spent the past year trying to knock state AI laws down in court — Executive Order 14365 (December 2025) created a Department of Justice AI Litigation Task Force for that purpose. Congress should not hand it a statutory veto.

**2. Section 111 (incident reporting): 72 hours, not 15 days.**

Please change Section 111's reporting clock to 72 hours, matching New York's RAISE Act (N.Y. Gen. Bus. Law § 1422), and keep the 24-hour duty for incidents posing an imminent risk of death or serious injury, extended to the law enforcement or public safety agency with jurisdiction, as California's law provides.

Fifteen days is a news cycle, not an early-warning system. If a frontier model's weights are stolen, or a risk control fails, the government and the public need to know while it still matters. We also ask that CAISI publish an annual public report summarizing incidents received, so Congress and the public can see patterns rather than single stories.

**3. Section 112 (audits): make them binding and pre-deployment.**

As drafted, IVOs verify compliance with a developer's paperwork on an ongoing basis. That is auditing the manual, not the machine. Please require that, before any frontier model is released, an IVO must verify that the model meets the developer's published framework and that the framework achieves an acceptable level of catastrophic risk mitigation — with the audit completed and filed with CAISI before deployment.

Finally, remove the blanket immunity for IVOs. A private firm paid by the company it audits should not be immune from claims when it misses a foreseeable catastrophic failure. Immunity weakens the incentive to be a good auditor. At minimum, condition immunity on audits that meet CAISI's standards and meet them independently, and require public summaries of audit findings so the public can see whether verification is real or a rubber stamp.

**4. Section 101 (definitions): set an objective safety standard, not a benefit-cost test.**

Section 101 defines an "acceptable level of catastrophic risk mitigation" as mitigation sufficient for a model's anticipated benefits to outweigh its level of catastrophic risk. That hands the judgment to the company: its own expected benefits, weighed against the public's safety. A frontier model is not a product whose risks a seller should be free to price in. Please replace this definition with an objective standard that CAISI sets and enforces.

**5. Section 113 (whistleblowers): protect people who report risk, not only people who report violations.**

Section 113 protects workers who report a violation of federal AI law. That is too narrow, and it is narrower than California's law. Please protect any worker — employee or independent contractor — who reports information they reasonably believe discloses a significant safety or health risk posed by a frontier model, or noncompliance with a safety framework, whether or not it is a violation of this Act (see Cal. Lab. Code § 1107.1). Add a civil penalty for retaliation. The people closest to these systems are the cheapest early-warning system the country has; the draft should not leave them afraid to use it.

**6. Add a federal licence for the largest training runs.**

The draft's own definition of a frontier model (Section 101) already identifies the systems we mean: models trained above a set computing-power threshold. Building one should require a licence. We ask you to add a licence requirement for training runs above that threshold, conditioned on a published safety framework, verified model-weight security, pre-deployment testing, and notice to CAISI before the run begins.

Without a licence there is no registry, and without a registry CAISI cannot monitor what it cannot see. We licence nuclear plants, aircraft manufacturers and drug makers because the downside is not bounded by what a company is willing to lose. Frontier AI is in that category. Today it is governed by an honor system, and voluntary commitments have not held.

**7. Section 102 (CAISI): codify it, then give it authority and money.**

We support codifying CAISI. But as drafted it writes voluntary guidelines, licenses auditors and receives reports. That is a standards body, not a regulator. Please add mandatory pre-deployment testing authority: CAISI should be able to obtain access to frontier models before release and test them for catastrophic risk, including loss-of-control potential, and its findings should be binding, not advisory.

The June 2026 executive order created a voluntary framework in which developers may let agencies review frontier models for up to 30 days before release. Voluntary is the operative word, and it is not enough. The United Kingdom's AI Security Institute has pre-deployment access to leading models and more than 100 technical specialists; we should match that, in law.

On funding, $100 million a year is nearly seven times CAISI's current $15 million appropriation, and we appreciate the seriousness of that. But treat it as a floor, not a ceiling. Ramp authorizations well above $100 million a year as the IVO regime scales, provide multi-year certainty so the institute can hire and keep technical staff, and do not treat IVO fees as a substitute for appropriations.

**8. Model-weight security: binding rules, not only a report.**

Section 321's report on model weight, data center and open-source security is welcome. Please pair it with binding model-weight security requirements as a condition of the licence proposed above. A stolen frontier model is a national security event, and right now the strongest federal protections are the ones a company volunteers to adopt.

**Closing**

We recognize that this draft is a genuine attempt to write federal AI law on a bipartisan basis, and that its sponsors are being pressured from every direction. Our position is simple and consistent: the systems that could cause catastrophic harm should face binding, enforceable safety requirements, and Congress must not wipe out the state laws that are today the only binding rules on the books. Sixty-six percent of voters say AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm. They expect rules with consequences, not guidelines.

Binding rules are not a brake on American innovation. They are the reason the public keeps letting this technology into its hospitals, its schools and its workplaces. We would welcome the chance to walk through these requests with your staff before introduction, and we are glad to supply the full topline results of our survey.

Respectfully,

**Dr. Miriam Achterberg**
Executive Director, Frontier Restraint Coalition
[email] | [phone]

# GREAT AMERICAN AI ACT: MAKE IT BINDING, NOT VOLUNTARY

**Frontier Restraint Coalition — E&C member briefing | October 2026**

**THE PROBLEM.** The most powerful AI systems could cause catastrophic harm, and leading AI scientists — including the heads of the labs — have warned the risk extends to human extinction (Statement on AI Risk, May 2023). The International AI Safety Report 2026 (100+ experts, 30+ countries) found models increasingly tell test settings from real deployment and find loopholes in evaluations, "which could allow dangerous capabilities to go undetected before deployment." These systems are being built faster than anyone can verify they are safe, and voluntary commitments have not held. 74% of voters want AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release (FRC survey, Aug 2026).

**WHERE THE DRAFT LANDS.** Reps. Obernolte and Trahan's draft takes real steps: published safety frameworks, independent audits, whistleblower protection, and codifying CAISI. But nobody has to *verify* a frontier model is safe before release — developers disclose their own risk assessments; auditors check paperwork on a schedule — and Section 121 would displace state laws that already go further.

**FIVE ASKS**

1. **Strike Section 121 (preemption).** It would displace California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act and Illinois' frontier safety law for three years — freezing the strongest binding rules in the country in the exact years they take effect. A federal standard should be a floor, not a ceiling.

2. **72-hour incident reporting (Section 111).** The draft allows 15 days. New York requires 72 hours; California requires 24 hours where there is an imminent risk of death. Fifteen days is a news cycle, not an early-warning system.

3. **Make audits pre-deployment and binding (Section 112).** Require verification against the developer's framework *before* each release, remove the blanket immunity for paid auditors, and publish audit summaries.

4. **Add a federal licence for the largest training runs.** Above the draft's own frontier-model threshold (Section 101): published safety framework, verified model-weight security, pre-deployment testing, notice to CAISI. No registry means nothing to monitor.

5. **Give CAISI real authority and real money (Section 102).** Mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for frontier models, and funding well above $100 million a year — treat $100 million as a floor, not a ceiling.

**WHY IT'S GOOD POLITICS.** 63% of voters say federal law should not block state AI safety laws. 66% say companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm.

**BOTTOM LINE.** Verify before deploy. Binding, not voluntary. A floor, not a ceiling.

# Staff Q&A — anticipated questions on the GAAIA discussion draft

Work order FRC-POL-2026-062 | Draft for Executive Director sign-off | 16 Oct 2026
For FRC spokespeople in Hill meetings. Each answer is under 120 words. Voice: plain language, no jargon, never guess at numbers.

---

**1. (Majority E&C staff) "The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?"**

Because it is after the fact, and mostly voluntary. Incident reporting is a smoke detector: it tells you the house is already on fire, and this draft's 15-day clock is weaker than New York's 72 hours. CAISI, as drafted, writes voluntary guidelines, licenses private auditors and receives reports. It cannot stop a release. The audits are paperwork checks rather than pre-deployment testing, and the auditors are immune when they miss something. Nothing in the bill requires a company to prove a frontier model is safe before it goes out. Give CAISI mandatory pre-deployment testing authority, a 72-hour clock, and a licence for the largest training runs — then this is a real framework, and we will say so.

**2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) "Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?"**

Dropped, yes — we could support the rest of the framework. Shortened, no: the length is not the problem. At any length, Section 121 turns a state floor into a federal ceiling, displacing California's SB 53 and New York's RAISE Act, including their 72-hour reporting standard. Our position is the Clean Air Act model — federal minimums, with states free to go further and to enforce. If sponsors insist on keeping a window, the federal standard must be at least as strong as SB 53 and the RAISE Act in every respect, and states must keep the right to act. Even then, three frozen years in this technology is a real cost, and we will say so.

**3. (Senate Commerce staff) "What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?"**

China is not an unregulated frontier. It requires algorithm filings and pre-deployment security assessments, has issued a stream of AI rules since 2025, and its policymakers are preparing for loss-of-control risk — Chinese and American experts largely agree on the risks. Second, these rules bind a handful of labs above the draft's own computing-power threshold; small and open-source developers are untouched. Third, frontier labs already comply with SB 53 and will comply with the RAISE Act, so a federal floor at that level costs them nothing new. And the race argument cuts the other way: the country that can prove its systems are safe is the country other governments, hospitals and militaries will trust.

**4. (Appropriations staff) "CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?"**

Codify it, and fund it well above $100 million a year — treat $100 million as a floor, not a ceiling. That is nearly seven times today's $15 million appropriation, and Rep. Franklin is already working to secure additional FY27 funding. But authority matters more than the number. As drafted, CAISI writes voluntary guidelines, licenses private auditors and receives reports; it cannot stop anything. The UK's AI Security Institute has pre-deployment access to leading models and more than 100 technical staff. We want that in statute: mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for frontier models, with findings that bind. Also urge multi-year authorizations so the institute can hire and keep technical people.
